name: Chilean Quechua
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Retired Glottolog/ISO entry (cqu merged into South Bolivian Quechua [quh], 2016); Glottolog lists no references for this languoid.

new_statements.quote: En general, el acento es penúltimo en la palabra —por ejemplo, kusikúni ‘estoy feliz’—, pero algunos sufijos finales requieren un acento final —por ejemplo, ¿qamrí? ‘¿y tú?’—. El acento también puede ser final en el caso que el morfema acusativo -ta se elide —por ejemplo, papá ‘papa, acusativo’ en contraste con papáta ‘papa, acusativo’ (Camacho Rios, 2023)—, o para indicar un sentido discursivo aún no bien entendido —por ejemplo, nuqáqa y nuqaqá ‘yo, tópico’—.
new_statements.translation: In general, stress is penultimate in the word (e.g. kusikúni 'I am happy'), but some final suffixes require final stress (e.g. ¿qamrí? 'and you?'). Stress can also be final when the accusative morpheme -ta is elided (e.g. papá 'potato, ACC' in contrast with papáta 'potato, ACC' (Camacho Rios 2023)), or to signal a discourse meaning not yet well understood (e.g. nuqáqa and nuqaqá 'I, topic').

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable; final stress only with a small set of final suffixes/enclitics (e.g. -rí), when an elided final suffix (-ta) leaves its stress behind, and in a discourse-conditioned alternation on topic -qa. This is the statement for South Bolivian Quechua, the language into which Chilean Quechua [cqu] was merged; no source describes stress from Chilean speakers' data.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Gallagher et al. 2024; Bills et al. 1969 (via SPA 1979) speaks only of primary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress with certain final suffixes (qamrí?), after elision of accusative -ta (papá < papáta), and discourse-conditioned nuqaqá; Bills et al. 1969 p.8 (via SPA): 'in a few (highly restricted) cases the primary stress falls on the final syllable'; Quiroz 2011 (catalog record for sout2991) adds -chá, -má always final and elided -taq.
new_statements.domain_note: Word domain ('en la palabra'), including suffixes; examples are inflected citation forms. Applies to chil1283 only by identity: ISO 639-3 CR 2015-024 / Glottolog treat Chilean Quechua as South Bolivian Quechua; Adelaar & Muysken 2004:188, Sichra 2009 and Lagos Fernandez 2025 describe the Antofagasta/Ollague Quechua as an extension of Potosi/Oruro/Cochabamba (Bolivian) Quechua; Chilean MINEDUC materials (Quispe et al. 2014; Programa 5o basico 2022) label the Ollague variety 'Cusco-Collao'. All Southern Quechua descriptions agree on penultimate stress.
new_statements.identity_note: chil1283 'Chilean Quechua' is a retired bookkeeping languoid: ISO 639-3 [cqu] was merged into South Bolivian Quechua [quh] (Glottolog sout2991) by CR 2015-024, effective 2016-01-15, on the grounds that no source records a separate Quechua language in Chile (Adelaar & Muysken 2004:188: 'an extension of the Bolivian variety'; Hammarstrom 2015). Every Chile-internal source opened agrees on the affiliation but none describes the phonology: Sichra 2009 (Atlas, t.2 p.48) and Lagos Fernandez 2025 (p.65) call the Antofagasta-oases/Ollague Quechua an extension of Potosi/Oruro/Cochabamba Quechua; Chilean MINEDUC materials made with Ollague speakers (Quispe, Urrelo & Morales 2014; Programa 5o basico 2022) label it 'variante Cusco-Collao' (i.e. Southern Quechua IIC). The quoted stress statement is therefore the South Bolivian Quechua statement (Gallagher et al. 2024, Cochabamba speakers), applied by identity. sout2991 is ALREADY in the catalog (webcat record, Quiroz Villarroel 2011, penultimate), so chil1283 should not become a separate catalog entity (retired code, same language) -- hence not proposed for the catalog despite a first-hand quote from a copies we hold. Pacheco Condori's Chile-published manual ('Todas las palabras son graves..', p.36) describes Cusco Quechua (cusc1236), not the Chilean community variety.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Southern Quechua is penultimate (Parker 1965, Adelaar 1984 y Palomino 1993). Similar statements have been made for South Bolivian Quechua (Bills G., et al 1971, Herrero & Sanchez 1978). Although, Plaza (2009:223) remarks on some exceptions to this penultimate default system. UPSBQ marks pitch accent in two ways: penultimate and final. The core stress is realized on the penultimate syllable. The second type corresponds to pitch accent in final syllable. This last one can be sub-divided into two: a phonemic final stress conditioned by certain morphemes that attract the pitch accent and a final stress conditioned by final suffix deletion rule. [...] Primary stress, secondary stress and intonation at a phrase level are still unexplored. (p. 65)
new_statements.citation: Camacho Rios, Gladys. 2022. [UT Austin PhD dissertation on South Bolivian Quechua, cited by Gallagher et al. 2024 as 'Camacho Rios 2023' for final stress under -ta elision]. Austin: University of Texas.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing statement (Gallagher, Huancacuri & Condori Arias 2024, p. 76: penultimate; final under some suffixes and under -ta elision), which in fact cites this dissertation for the -ta elision case. Adds the -rpa-n CCVC case, the topicalizer =qa and negative =chu deletions, and names the enclitics =chá and =rí. Describes Uma Piwra Quechua (UPSBQ), a rural monolingual variety of South Bolivian Quechua in Cochabamba department, Bolivia; Chile is not mentioned anywhere in the text (0 hits).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the penultimate syllable (maki ['ma.ki], pilipintu [pi.li.'pin.tu], purini [pu.'ri.ni]). Final stress arises (a) with inherently accented enclitics, the dubitative =chá and interrogative =rí (pp. 66-67); (b) with the suffix -rpa 'suddenly' + 3SG -n, giving a stressed heavy CCVC final syllable (saru-rpa-n [sa.ru.'rpan], p. 67), described as uncommon and not standard SBQ; and (c) when a monosyllabic final suffix is deleted after penultimate stress has been assigned (accusative -ta, topicalizer =qa, negative =chu; e.g. papá for papa-ta, p. 68).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described: 'Primary stress, secondary stress and intonation at a phrase level are still unexplored' (p. 65).
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress with enclitics =chá and =rí; final stress on -rpa-n (heavy CCVC final syllable); final stress from deletion of monosyllabic suffixes -ta, =qa, =chu; also cites Plaza (2009:223) for exceptions to the penultimate default.
new_statements.identity_note: chil1283 is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid (ISO [cqu] merged into [quh] South Bolivian Quechua, 2016). Camacho Rios 2022 describes Uma Piwra Quechua (UPSBQ), the speech of monolingual elders in a rural village in Cochabamba department, Bolivia; it never mentions Chile. The earlier passes record that the Quechua of Antofagasta/Ollague (Chile) is treated in the literature as an extension of Bolivian (Potosi/Oruro/Cochabamba) Quechua, and that Chilean teaching materials use Cuzco-Collao Quechua; no first-hand phonological description of Quechua as spoken in Chile was found in the compilation.

new_statements.quote: [p.188] Larraı́n Barros (1991) mentions the presence of Quechua speakers in the Chilean province of Antofagasta, in the Atacama desert oases of Ayquina, Cupo, Toconce and Turi. There are no specific data on this dialect, but it is likely to be an extension of the Bolivian variety of Quechua. [p.206] In most Quechua dialects stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of each polysyllabic word form and thus provides an easy phonology-based criterion for word delimitation. Exceptionally, in interjections and emphatic expressions, stress can be word-final, e.g. in alaláw ‘how cold!’.

new_statements.relation_note: No catalog record for chil1283; the two statements held by the project (Gallagher et al. 2024; Camacho Rios 2022) give penultimate stress with restricted final stress for South Bolivian Quechua. Adelaar & Muysken's general Quechua rule (penultimate; exceptional final stress in interjections/emphatics) matches; the book adds explicitly that nothing specific is known about the Chilean (Antofagasta) variety and that it is presumably Bolivian Quechua.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The book has no phonological data specific to the Quechua of the Antofagasta oases (Chile) and treats it as a likely extension of (South) Bolivian Quechua; for Quechua generally, and Bolivian Quechua is not among the listed deviant dialects, stress falls on the penultimate vowel of every polysyllabic word, with word-final stress only exceptionally in interjections and emphatic expressions.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing said about secondary stress for Quechua II / Bolivian Quechua
new_statements.exceptions: word-final stress in interjections and emphatic expressions (alaláw 'how cold!'); word-final stress from elision of a final syllable in Tarma / northern Junin (quantity-insensitive) and Pacaraos (akšú-k < akšú-kta), quantity-insensitive word-final first-person long vowel (wasí-: 'my house'), phonemic stress in Pacaraos, weight/initial patterns in Ancash (Huaraz), Cajatambo, Ferreñafe, Amazonas -- none of these concern Bolivian/Chilean Quechua
new_statements.identity_note: chil1283 'Chilean Quechua' is a retired bookkeeping languoid (ISO cqu merged into quh South Bolivian Quechua, 2016). Adelaar & Muysken 2004 p.188 locate it in the Atacama oases of Ayquina, Cupo, Toconce and Turi (Antofagasta province) after Larraín Barros 1991 and call it a likely extension of Bolivian Quechua, with no data of its own; their stress statement is for Quechua dialects generally (deviant systems named only for Pacaraos, Ancash/Huaraz, Cajatambo, Ferreñafe, Amazonas, Tarma/N Junín, none Bolivian). Bills et al. 1969 teach Cochabamba (South Bolivian) Quechua. So every stress statement available for chil1283 is a South Bolivian Quechua statement applied by extension.

new_statements.relation_note: No catalog record for chil1283; agrees with both statements held by the project (penultimate default, restricted final stress incl. -rí forms). The book describes Cochabamba (South Bolivian) Quechua, of which the retired Chilean Quechua languoid [cqu -> quh 2016] is the Chilean extension; it says nothing about Chile.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress in (Cochabamba/Bolivian) Quechua is almost always penultimate; in a few highly restricted cases it is final, and the course marks those with an acute accent (arí 'yes', tatáy, qanrí -- the last shows the final-stressed topic/question enclitic -rí also cited by Gallagher et al. 2024 as qamrí).
